strings.path.title: Shred
strings.path.goal: Alternate, economy, legato, sweeps and tapping in A minor, built up one technique at a time, finishing with an eight-bar sixteenth-note run over a band at 100 BPM.
strings.path.assumes: You can alternate-pick the A minor pentatonic box and a three-notes-per-string run in sixteenths at 80 BPM (Alternate Picking through its Intermediate Level covers this). The first two Levels take the crossings and the three-notes-per-string shape of Alternate Picking to higher tempos and add new drills between them, including speed bursts. The minutes are one pass through the material; the drills are meant to be repeated for weeks, and their variants change keys and strings so the repetition stays fresh.
strings.path.gradingLimits: Picked single notes, sixteenths to about 120 BPM and sextuplets to about 90, are the case the app is built for: timing evenness, notes heard and extra notes, plus right notes where the notes are at least 75 ms apart and the pitch is clear, after the take. None of it has been tried on a real guitar. Legato: a hammer-on or pull-off the app doesn't hear costs nothing, so the timing leans on the picked notes and the volume of the legato notes is a self-check; a hammer-on from nowhere and a tap count as attacks that must be heard. Sweeps are graded on timing only: swept notes ring into each other, right notes mostly read 'not checked', and their titles say so; only rungs with at least 150 ms between notes are graded. Accents are rough, louder or not. Pick direction is never heard: it is a checklist item wherever the strokes matter. Above sixteenths at 100 BPM, read the timing as provisional until the input delay is calibrated, and use a clean or light-crunch tone for graded takes.
strings.path.skills.1: Sixteenth notes with a click at 80 BPM
strings.step.one-string.title: One-string sixteenths
strings.step.one-string.goal: Four notes to every click on one string, even, at 100 BPM and then on toward 120.
strings.step.one-string.why: Every fast line in this Path is this motion with something added: a crossing, a shape, a legato note. On one string there is nothing to hide behind, so an uneven stroke shows up at once, and it is the cheapest place to fix it. Sixteenths at 110 to 120 is where most players' picking either becomes a motion they trust or starts to lock up.
strings.step.one-string.howTo.0: Count '1 e and a': down on 1 and 'and', up on 'e' and 'a'. Every Exercise in this Step is sixteenth notes, four to each click.
strings.step.one-string.howTo.1: Pick from the wrist, small. If the forearm locks, drop one rung: the locked arm is the usual speed wall, not the fingers.
strings.step.one-string.howTo.2: Keep down and up strokes the same loudness. Uneven pick depth is the most common reason they are not.
strings.step.one-string.payoff: Two bars of open-string sixteenths that sound like a machine, and a one-string lick at fret 12 that already sounds like shred.

strings.exercise.one-string.open-a.coachLine: This one is only about time. I'll say how even your best eight bars in a row were and whether any note went missing.

strings.exercise.one-string.four-of-each.title: Four of each, on the top string
strings.exercise.one-string.four-of-each.purpose: A melody where the fretting hand moves once a beat and the pick never stops: the rate in the right hand, the music in the left.
strings.exercise.one-string.four-of-each.howTo.0: Sixteenths, four per note, on the top string: A, C, B, A, then G, A, B, C. Move the fretting hand exactly on the beat, not a hair before.
strings.exercise.one-string.four-of-each.howTo.1: This is tremolo picking in slow motion, and a good first thing to play on any day.

strings.step.accents.title: Accents and groupings
strings.step.accents.goal: Put the accent where the music wants it, on a downstroke or an upstroke, in sextuplets and across the beat, without the time moving.
strings.step.accents.why: Fast playing is heard in groups, not notes: a run of sextuplets sounds like shred only when the first of every six is stronger. Accents also prove the picking hand is under control rather than running on its own, and an accent on an upstroke is the honest test of that.
strings.step.accents.howTo.0: An accent is a little more depth and speed in one stroke. Don't squeeze, and keep the unaccented notes quiet on purpose: the contrast makes the accent.
strings.step.accents.howTo.1: Sextuplets are six notes to the click, two groups of three: say 'one-trip-let-two-trip-let'. Sixteenths are four to the click.
strings.step.accents.howTo.2: Use a clean or light-crunch tone. Compression and high gain flatten accents, for your ear and for the app.
strings.step.accents.payoff: The same notes that sounded like a typewriter now have a pulse, and a six-note figure rolls against the beat the way it does on the records.

strings.exercise.accents.walking-accent.howTo.0: Sixteenths on fret 7 of the G string. Bar 1 accents the first of each four, bar 2 the second, bar 3 the third, bar 4 the fourth. Keep the time dead still at each change.
strings.exercise.accents.walking-accent.coachLin: Bars 2 and 4 are the test. The accent reading is rough, so trust your ear too.

strings.step.crossing.title: Crossing two strings
strings.step.crossing.goal: Change strings at sixteenths with no gap and no scrape, on both kinds of crossing.
strings.step.crossing.why: These are the two crossings from Alternate Picking, now in moving pairs and a lick. On one string the pick has nothing in its way; between two strings it has to get over one of them. There are only two kinds of crossing, and every line in the rest of this Path is built from them: outside, where the pick travels around the pair, and inside, where it is trapped between the strings and has to escape.
strings.step.crossing.howTo.0: Outside: a downstroke on the lower-pitched string, then an upstroke on the higher one. Each stroke starts from outside the pair.
strings.step.crossing.howTo.1: Inside: an upstroke on the lower-pitched string, then a downstroke on the higher one. Each stroke starts between the two strings, so the pick must hop out of the gap.
strings.step.crossing.howTo.2: Much of this motion is a small tilt of the wrist. Try it slowly with no click first, then sixteenths with the click.
strings.step.crossing.payoff: A short A minor lick that used to trip every time now rolls, and you can name which crossing is the one that catches you.
strings.exercise.crossing.outside-pairs.title: Outside pairs on G and B
strings.exercise.crossing.outside-pairs.purpose: Moving pairs of notes, all outside crossings, so the fretting hand gets busier while the pick path never changes.
strings.exercise.crossing.outside-pairs.howTo.0: Sixteenths. Two of each pair, then change: in A minor, C and E, D and G, C and F, D and E. The strokes never change: down on the G string, up on the B string.
strings.exercise.crossing.outside-pairs.coachLin: I can time these and check the notes. Which way the pick went is yours to keep honest, so the checklist asks.

strings.exercise.crossing.outside-pairs.cue.1: Pick both strings of every pair.
strings.exercise.crossing.outside-pairs.cue.2: Keep the stroke small: just the two strings.
strings.exercise.crossing.outside-pairs.cue.3: Look at the next pair a beat ahead.
strings.exercise.crossing.outside-pairs.cue.4: Put each new pair right on the beat.
strings.exercise.crossing.outside-pairs.cue.5: Wait for the click before each new pair.
strings.exercise.crossing.outside-pairs.cue.6: Keep the pick close as you cross.

strings.step.chromatic.title: Petrucci chromatic and the spider
strings.step.chromatic.goal: One finger per fret across all six strings, even at sixteenths, with the hand moving up the neck.
strings.step.chromatic.why: Chromatic drills are not music, and that is why they work: there is no tune to carry you, so every weak finger and every awkward string change is exposed. Ten minutes of this a day is the classic way to make the fourth finger as useful as the first and to make string changes stop being events.
strings.step.chromatic.howTo.0: One finger per fret: first finger on the lowest fret of the four, little finger on the highest. Keep the fingers close to the strings, curved, tips down.
strings.step.chromatic.howTo.1: Sixteenths throughout, four to the click.
strings.step.chromatic.howTo.2: Thumb behind the neck, relaxed. If it squeezes, the little finger tires first.
strings.step.chromatic.howTo.3: Stop at any pain in the hand, wrist or forearm. A tired forearm is one thing and pain is another; pain ends the set.
strings.step.chromatic.payoff: Your little finger keeps up, and a six-string crawl that used to stumble at the B string now sounds like one line.

strings.step.gilbert.title: Gilbert pentatonic crossings
strings.step.gilbert.goal: Loop a two-string pentatonic figure in sextuplets, then move it down the box, without the crossing ever catching.
strings.step.gilbert.why: Two notes on each of two strings, looped, is the figure behind a great deal of fast rock soloing: it sounds wild and is only four frets. It is also the purest inside-crossing drill there is, because every string change in the six-note loop is inside. Learn it here and the pentatonic box stops being something you walk through and becomes something you can play fast.
strings.step.gilbert.howTo.0: The box is A minor pentatonic at fret 5: first finger on fret 5, third or little finger on the upper note of each string.
strings.step.gilbert.howTo.1: Sextuplets: six to the click. The six-note loop fills one beat exactly, so the loop starts on every click.
strings.step.gilbert.howTo.2: Keep the crossings small. The pick only has to clear one string; most of the miss comes from swinging too wide.
strings.step.gilbert.payoff: A blurring pentatonic loop at a tempo you can play in a solo, and the same loop on any pair of strings in the box.

strings.exercise.gilbert.six-loop.howTo.1: Down, up, down, up, down, up: six is even, so every loop starts on a downstroke.

strings.step.three-per-string.title: Three notes per string
strings.step.three-per-string.goal: Run A minor in three-note-per-string shapes at sixteenths, where the crossing changes type at every string.
strings.step.three-per-string.why: This is the shape from Alternate Picking, at a higher tempo, and the six-note licks are now in sixteenths. An odd number of notes per string flips the stroke at each change, so outside and inside crossings take turns. This is the shape of most fast scalar playing: a long scale with no position shift to manage, and the same fingering idea on every string.
strings.step.three-per-string.howTo.0: Each string has three notes, fretted 1-2-4 or 1-3-4 depending on the gaps. Open the hand from the first finger; don't twist the wrist to reach.
strings.step.three-per-string.howTo.1: Sixteenths throughout, four to the click, so the string changes fall in different places in the beat. Count the beat, not the strings.
strings.step.three-per-string.howTo.2: Ascending, the changes go outside, inside, outside. Say which one is next until you stop needing to.
strings.step.three-per-string.payoff: A two-and-a-half-octave A minor run, and a six-note lick you will use for the rest of your life.

strings.step.sequences.title: Three-per-string sequences
strings.step.sequences.goal: Play A minor in groups of three, four and six, so the scale becomes phrases rather than a staircase.
strings.step.sequences.why: Nobody plays a scale straight up in a solo. Sequences are how a scale turns into lines: each group starts one note further on, and the ear hears the pattern rather than the notes. The group size is matched to the rhythm (threes as triplets, fours as sixteenths, sixes as sextuplets) so the group always starts on the beat.
strings.step.sequences.howTo.0: Learn each sequence slowly by saying the first note of each group. If you lose the first note, you have lost the sequence.
strings.step.sequences.howTo.1: Each Exercise names its rhythm: triplets are three to the click, sixteenths four, sextuplets six.
strings.step.sequences.howTo.2: The fingering is the three-notes-per-string shape from the last Step. Don't change it to make a group easier.
strings.step.sequences.payoff: 'A minor in fours' up and down, and a six-note sequence in sextuplets that sounds like a real run.

strings.step.speed-bursts.title: Speed bursts
strings.step.speed-bursts.goal: Play short runs above your clean tempo and land on time, without tensing up for the whole bar.
strings.step.speed-bursts.why: You can't practise speed by doing everything slowly and you can't do it by flailing. A burst is the honest middle: one beat of real speed, then a rest long enough that the hand lets go. Most players find a burst runs several rungs above what they can sustain, which tells them the wall is stamina or tension rather than how fast the fingers can go.
strings.step.speed-bursts.howTo.0: Rest between bursts. The rest is half the Exercise: let the hand go soft before the next one.
strings.step.speed-bursts.howTo.1: Aim at the landing note, not at the run. If you land on time, the run was fine.
strings.step.speed-bursts.howTo.2: Sixteenths in the bursts, sextuplets in the last one; the tempos here are well above the last Steps on purpose.
strings.step.speed-bursts.payoff: You will hear yourself play a short run far faster than you thought you could, and it will be clean.

strings.step.string-skipping.title: String skipping
strings.step.string-skipping.goal: Keep strict alternate picking going when the line jumps over a string, in octaves, pentatonics and a triad.
strings.step.string-skipping.why: So far every crossing has been to a neighbour. A skip makes the pick aim: it has to travel over a string it must not touch and arrive on time. Skipping is also where a lot of the modern shred sound comes from, because wide intervals on adjacent beats sound like nothing a scale can do.
strings.step.string-skipping.howTo.0: On a skip, let the pick travel in a small arc over the string in between. Do not lift the whole forearm.
strings.step.string-skipping.howTo.1: Mute the skipped string with the side of the picking hand and a spare fretting finger. Noise appears on skips before it appears anywhere else.
strings.step.string-skipping.payoff: Octaves climbing the neck, a pentatonic line that leaps instead of walking, and an A minor triad that sounds like a sweep but is picked.

strings.exercise.string-skipping.octaves.howTo.1: A small shift each beat, up the scale in bar 1 and back in bar 2.
strings.exercise.string-skipping.octaves.howTo.2: Muting is the technique here: the underside of the first finger damps the string between the octave notes, and the picking hand's palm damps the strings below.
strings.exercise.string-skipping.octaves.coachLi: If notes go missing here it is usually the skip or the shift. Slow down until neither is a surprise.

strings.step.economy.title: Economy picking
strings.step.economy.goal: Alternate on a string, and let the pick carry straight through to the next string when it is already travelling that way.
strings.step.economy.why: Strict alternate picking spends a stroke getting back over a string every time a three-note group changes string. Economy picking keeps going instead: the downstroke that ends one string falls through onto the next. Many shred players mix the two, and a five-note group is where economy picking shines, because the strokes come out the same on every repeat.

strings.step.economy.howTo.2: Don't let the push turn into a strum: the pick rests against the next string for an instant, then plays it, exactly in time.
strings.step.economy.payoff: A three-string run that feels lighter than it did alternate-picked, and a five-note figure in quintuplets that rolls on its own.

strings.step.legato-one.title: Legato I: trills and pulls
strings.step.legato-one.goal: Hammer-ons and pull-offs as loud and as even as picked notes, tied to a picked note on the beat.
strings.step.legato-one.why: Legato is the other half of shred: the fretting hand plays most of the notes and the pick only marks the time. It sounds smooth only when the hammered notes are as strong as the picked ones, which is a strength and accuracy problem for the fretting hand. Every legato bar here comes after a picked bar of the same notes, so the picked bar sets the sound and the rhythm the legato bar has to match.
strings.step.legato-one.howTo.0: Hammer from a little height with the fingertip, and land exactly on the beat's subdivision. Pull off slightly sideways, toward the floor, so the string is plucked and not just released.

strings.step.legato-one.howTo.2: Mute the strings you are not playing with the picking hand: legato rings the open strings more than picking does.
strings.step.legato-one.payoff: A trill that sounds like one note shimmering, and a pentatonic waterfall of pull-offs in sextuplets.

strings.step.sweep-basics.title: Sweep basics (timing only)
strings.step.sweep-basics.goal: One continuous push of the pick through two and three strings, separate notes, nothing ringing, and a turn at the top.
strings.step.sweep-basics.why: A sweep is one motion that plays several notes, which is why it is not alternate picking done faster. The smallest sweep, two strings, contains the whole technique and the whole problem: if the first note keeps ringing, you get a chord. The app grades these on timing only: swept notes ring into each other, so right notes mostly read 'not checked', and nothing here promises them.
strings.step.sweep-basics.howTo.0: One push from the arm, the wrist quiet. The pick comes to rest on the next string between notes, then falls through it. This is the stroke from the Step 'Economy picking', carried across more strings.
strings.step.sweep-basics.howTo.1: Fretting hand: as soon as the next note sounds, release the last one without leaving the string. That is the mute that does most of the work.
strings.step.sweep-basics.howTo.2: Eighth-note triplets throughout, three to the click.
strings.step.sweep-basics.payoff: A three-string A minor arpeggio that comes out of one stroke, turns at the top without a seam, and a two-string lick you can drop into a solo.
strings.exercise.sweep-basics.two-string-rolls.p: Down through two strings at the same fret, rest, then up through them: the push, and the fingertip roll that keeps two notes from ringing.
strings.exercise.sweep-basics.two-string-rolls.h: Eighth-note triplets: two notes down, a rest, two notes up, a rest. One finger covers both strings and rolls so only the sounding note is pressed.
Down is one push through both strings; up is one pull back through them.

strings.step.five-string-sweeps.goal: The three-string loop with a turn at the top, the classic five-string A minor sweep from fret 12, and the link from one shape into the next.
strings.step.five-string-sweeps.why: Five strings is the big sweep, the sound people mean by the word. It is only worth having if it connects: a progression doesn't wait while you find the next shape, so the link from one arpeggio into the next is practised as its own skill. As before, these are graded on timing only.
strings.step.five-string-sweeps.howTo.0: Mute everything. With five strings moving there is more to keep silent than there are fingers: palm on the low strings, fretting fingers across the high ones.
strings.step.five-string-sweeps.howTo.1: A link is one small move of the fretting hand on the top or bottom string: a hammer, a pull or a slide into the next chord's nearest note. The pick does nothing at that moment.
strings.step.five-string-sweeps.howTo.2: Eighth-note triplets throughout, three to the click.
strings.step.five-string-sweeps.payoff: A five-string arpeggio up the strings and back with every note separate, and two shapes joined with no gap at the bar line.

strings.step.tapping-etude.title: Tapping, then the etude
strings.step.tapping-etude.goal: Tap a triplet arpeggio with the picking hand over the chords, hold a line for a minute, then play an eight-bar run over the band.
strings.step.tapping-etude.why: Tapping adds notes no fretting hand could reach, and over chord changes it sounds bigger than anything else in this Path for the effort. Then the finale: a minute of unbroken sixteenths shows whether the speed is built on tension, and an eight-bar run with a band is the reason you did all the rest.
strings.step.tapping-etude.howTo.0: Tap with the middle finger of the picking hand, holding the pick tucked away. Tap hard and pull off slightly downward so the next note sounds. The tab marks a tap T.
strings.step.tapping-etude.howTo.1: Taps are the loud notes and the timing is read from them most firmly. The pulled and hammered notes between them may be too quiet to catch, and cost nothing if they are.
strings.step.tapping-etude.howTo.2: Stop at any pain in the hand, wrist or forearm. A tired forearm is one thing and pain is another; pain ends the set.
strings.step.tapping-etude.payoff: A tapped arpeggio that moves with the chords, a full minute of sixteenths that sounds the same at the end as at the start, and an eight-bar run over a band.

strings.exercise.tapping-etude.tap-triplets.howT: Eighth-note triplets, three to the click. The picking hand taps on every click; the fretting hand holds the low note with the first finger and hammers the middle note with the ring or little finger (top string 12-5-8, B string 17-10-13, G string 14-5-9).
Mute: the fretting hand's first finger lies lightly across the higher strings, and the picking hand's palm rests on the low strings while it taps.

strings.level.advanced.title: Advanced: legato, sweeps, tapping and the band
strings.level.advanced.summary: Legato tied to picked notes, sweeps graded on timing only, tapping over chords, a stamina minute and the eight-bar run. Legato, Sweep Picking and Tapping teach these techniques from the first note. This Level is the short version, for joining them to your picking.
strings.level.advanced.startHereIf.0: You can run A minor three notes per string across three strings at sixteenths, 95 BPM.
